The aesthetic experience of interior spaces with curvilinear boundaries and various
space properties in immersive and desktop-based virtual environments
Tugce Elver Boz1, Halime Demirkan1, Burcu A. Urgen2, 3, 4
1Department of Interior Architecture and Environmental Design, I.D. Bilkent University,
Faculty of Art, Design and Architecture, Ankara, Turkey.
2Department of Psychology, I.D. Bilkent University, Faculty of Economics, Administrative and
Social Sciences, Ankara, Turkey.
3Interdisciplinary Neuroscience Graduate Program, I.D. Bilkent University, Graduate School
of Science and Engineering, Ankara, Turkey.
4Aysel Sabuncu Brain Research Center and National Magnetic Resonance Research Center
(UMRAM), I.D. Bilkent University, Ankara, Turkey.
Corresponding authors:
E-mail addresses: tugce.elver@bilkent.edu.tr (Tugce Elver Boz), burcu.urgen@bilkent.edu.tr
(Burcu A. Urgen), demirkan@bilkent.edu.tr (Halime Demirkan)
Tel: +90 530 155 09 71

Abstract
The present study aims to investigate aesthetic experience in response to environments with
curvilinear boundaries in two different virtual environments (VEs), namely immersive (IVE)
and desktop-based virtual environments (DTVE). To this end, 60 participants were presented
with 360-degree 32 VE visualizations that had horizontal or vertical curved boundaries and
possessed various architectural properties including size, light, texture, and color, using a head-
mounted display and a desktop computer. The aesthetic experience was measured in terms of
three key dimensions identified before (Elver Boz et al., 2022): familiarity, excitement, and
fascination. In addition, participants' sense of presence was measured. The results show that
familiarity and excitement dimensions were significantly higher in IVE than in DTVE, whereas
the two environments did not differ from each other in terms of fascination. As for the boundary
types, familiarity was significantly higher in horizontal boundaries than in vertical ones. In
contrast, excitement and fascination were significantly higher in vertical than in horizontal
boundaries. The only dimension that showed an interaction between the boundary and the
virtual environment was excitement. Finally, IVE induced a higher presence feeling than
DTVE. These results have important implications for researchers who study aesthetic
experiences using immersive virtual reality or 2D images.
Keywords: Virtual environment, Immersive environments, Aesthetic experience

The aesthetic experience of interior spaces with curvilinear boundaries and various
space properties in immersive and desktop-based virtual environments
1. Introduction
With the development of virtual reality (VR) technology, the awareness of virtual built
environment systems increased rapidly. The game industry and the education, design,
architecture, and construction sectors have used this technology dynamically. When applied to
a built environment, the most significant feature of VR is its ability to provide users with a
sense of immersion and presence. The idea of VR systems in built environments is to describe
and resemble architectural environments that do not exist in reality (Bertol, 1997). It enables
designers to examine the environment in many aspects before construction.
VR systems include many components in one area, such as a three-dimensional (3D)
model, displays, interaction devices, and software (Paes et al., 2023). There are many types to
express the 3D model, which can be immersive or non-immersive. The immersive virtual
environments represent the high-end system; sensors track the user's movements in the real
world while the display delivers stereoscopic views of a model. The non-immersive virtual
environments represent the low-end system. The display mode offers monoscopic views of a
digital model, and interaction devices are limited to a simple mouse and keyboard (Bertol,
1997).
With the development of new technology, many scholars have recently investigated
stereoscopic and monoscopic displays of perception and presence factors in built environments
(Paes et al., 2017; Paes et al., 2021; Paes et al., 2023). This study also investigates the
relationship between 3D immersive and desktop-based perception and presence in curvilinear
boundaries with various space properties in the virtual environment. Using the VR system in
this research easily enables the modification of different variables to understand the effect on
1

people's perception and presence. Besides, the key architectural aesthetic dimensions, namely
familiarity, excitement, and fascination, are evaluated for each space, as Elver Boz et al. (2022)
emphasized a comprehensive framework to characterize human aesthetic experience in a VR
environment.
2. Literature review
2.1. Architectural Aesthetic Experience
Many studies emphasized that architecture's aesthetic qualities greatly impact people's
cognitive assessment, emotional well-being, and behavioral approach (Adams, 2014; Cooper et
al., 2014; Gifford, 2002; Hartig, 2008; Joye, 2007). In the literature, several theoretical models
specify various components in explaining the importance of architectural aesthetic experience
(Chatterjee & Vartanian, 2014, 2016; Coburn et al., 2017; Coburn et al., 2020; Elver Boz et al.,
2022; Hekkert, 2006; Leder et al., 2004).
Chatterjee and Vartanian (2014) propose an aesthetic triad model of architectural
experience and aim to provide a broader framework in the aesthetic field. The triad model
created by Chatterjee and Vartanian (2014) and its extension by Coburn et al. (2020), in which
aesthetic experience is characterized by separate cognitive, emotional, and behavioral elements,
has a more holistic approach based on these broad domains in psychology.
Coburn et al. (2020) extend Chatterjee and Vartanian's (2014) aesthetic triad model and
adapts three important domains in this model: cognition associated with knowledge-meaning,
the emotion associated with the emotion-valuation, and behavior that is linked to the
sensorimotor system. Correspondingly, their study investigates more than a hundred real
interior images comprising various space variables (ceiling height, enclosure, and curvature).
Their study identified three key aesthetic components that are (1) coherence; the ease with
2

which one organizes and comprehends a scene, (2) fascination; a scene's informational richness
and generated interest; and (3) hominess; the extent to which a scene reflects a personal space.
Elver Boz et al. (2022) studied a comprehensive and empirically driven framework that
characterizes human aesthetic experience for architectural spaces. Their study aims to reveal
key dimensions of aesthetic experience and how various properties of the built environment
affect these dimensions. Instead of real environment images, they created 3D 360-degree
simulations of different architectural variables and in order not to lose controlling factors with
other elements such as the furniture layout, form, and color of the furniture, the view of the
window openings, sunlight coming from the outside, or mural compositions, study conducted
with an empty space. By leveraging virtual reality, they systematically manipulated various
space variables (curvilinear boundaries and four space properties; size, light, texture, and color).
Their findings suggest that human aesthetic experience in spaces with curvilinear boundaries
can be reduced to three key dimensions, namely (1) familiarity, (2) excitement, and (3)
fascination, and different architectural properties affect these dimensions differently. The study
shows that aesthetic experience for architectural spaces with curvilinear boundaries can be
characterized by three key dimensions, which include elements that overlap between Chatterjee
and Vartanian’s (2014) cognitive, emotional, and behavioral elements of the triad model.
Elver Boz et al. (2022) described three key aesthetic dimensions as follows: Familiarity as
“How pleased, satisfied or relaxed one feels in an environment, how safe and coherent they
think the environment looks, and how they would like to behave in this environment such as
whether they would like to spend time or enjoy exploring.” (p.10); excitement as “How excited,
frenzied, jittery or contended one feels in an environment.” (p.10); and fascination is “How
mysterious or complex an environment looks or how stimulated one feels in that environment.”
(p.10).
3

2.2. Virtual Environment as an Architectural Design Support Tool
Much research investigates people's responses between virtual and real environments by
comparing cognitive judgment, emotional well-being, and behavioral approaches. De Kort et
al. (2003) found that behavioral experience in virtual environments is similar to that in real
environments, but there are also modest significant differences in environmental evaluations as
height perception of a room. Kuliga et al. (2015) found few statistically significant differences
between real and virtual building ratings. Their analyses based on qualitative data revealed
differences relating to atmospherics. The main conclusion of this study is that VR has a strong
potential to be used as a practical research tool in psychological and architectural research and
that future studies could supplement behavioral validation. Besides Brade et al. (2017)
emphasized that virtual and real environments presence and user experience factors were
correlated. The idea of the Brade et al. (2017) study indicates that VE can be an alternative to
the real environment for user experience when a high presence is achieved.
2.3. Immersive Virtual Environment (IVE) and Desktop-based Virtual Environment
(DTVE)
VR is the technology that immerses a person into a three-dimensional computer-generated
simulated environment (Sherman & Craig, 2003). It enables users to immerse virtually in
spaces, defining the boundaries of an immersive architectural environment that imitates that of
a visual living space. Therefore, it enables one to walk through space as if in the existing
location. Implementing environmental properties like size, light, texture, and color to the
boundaries of that space helps to create the viewer's sense of place within the environment,
enriching the experience by enhancing engagement and meaning for the viewer more than a
three-dimensional space. Making sense of place within a virtual environment must draw
attention to the sensations, feelings, thoughts, and emotions of viewers of that space. Executing
this within a space includes employing recognizable elements within the design of boundaries
4

of the surrounding environment. Virtual environment boundaries should be carefully designed
to achieve the most significant understanding and knowledge gain for the viewer regarding the
spatial world.
In the literature, many examples of virtual environments can be experienced using
immersive displays (e.g., head-mounted displays-HMD) or non-immersive displays (e.g.,
desktop computers). In each virtual environment, the participants could have different
experiences and results based on the spatial characteristics of the virtual environment. Paes et
al. (2017) compared spatial user perception between immersive and traditional (conventional
workstation) virtual environment systems. Results indicate a better spatial perception of the
virtual model when using an immersive environment than the traditional one. The study
concludes that the immersive environment may benefit current design practices by improving
professionals' understanding of the spatial arrangement of the virtual model. Paes et al. (2021)
also compared perception and presence between immersive (HMD), non-immersive (laptop
monitor) virtual environments, and physical environments (real environment). The result of the
study showed that immersive VR systems provide a greater presence than non-immersive ones.
Also, an immersive system provides a more immersive experience, benefits collaborative
design review, and increases productivity. Paes et al. (2023) investigated the relationship
between the physical and virtual environments (non-immersive and immersive) in perception
and presence in virtual reality-reconstructed architecture. According to the study, Higuera-
Trujillo et al. (2017) investigated the psychological and physiological responses evoked by
three environments: real photographs, 360-degree panoramas, and VR, as well as the users'
sense of presence. They found that 360-degree panoramas enable the closest results to reality
based on the participants' psychological responses and VR based on the physiological
responses. As a result, they concluded that researchers could use 360-degree VR environments
to replicate the experiences in physical environments. Shu et al. (2019) investigate whether VR
5

appears or feels different to users when different virtual environments are used (HMD and
desktop computer) in terms of sense of presence. As a result, users indicated a higher sense of
spatial presence and immersion while using VR HMD than desktop VR.
The present study investigates whether a VE (immersive virtual environment-IVE and
desktop-based virtual environment-DTVE) affects the aesthetic experience dimensions of the
participants in a space with curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties (size,
light, texture, and color). The study also intends to analyze the effects of IVE and DTVE on
participants' sense of presence. Participants rated these VEs based on the findings of Elver Boz
et al.’s (2022) research that defined the three dimensions of aesthetic experience; familiarity,
excitement, and fascination.
The following research questions (RQ) are posed:
RQ 1. What are the aesthetic experience dimensions associated with virtual environments (VEs)
and curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties of interior spaces?
RQ 2. Is there a difference in aesthetic experience dimensions based on VEs of interior spaces?
RQ 3. Is there a difference in aesthetic experience dimensions based on curvilinear boundaries
with various architectural properties of interior spaces?
RQ 4. Does interaction between VEs and curvilinear boundaries with various architectural
properties affect the aesthetic experience dimensions of interior spaces?
RQ 5. Is there a difference in presence based on VEs of interior spaces?
RQ 6. Do aesthetic experience dimensions have an impact on the presence scores in VE?
6

3. Method
3.1. Participants
I. D. Bilkent University Institutional Ethical Review Board approved this study (No:
2018_01_18_04). All the participants signed the informed consent form that stated the purposes
of the study and explained the participants’ involvement as well as the risk and emergency
procedures. Based on a priori G* Power F-test analysis for ANOVA: Repeated measures, within
factors, were conducted using computed effect size (f) 0.25, α=0.05, and a power level of 0.90
(Cohen, 1988), indicating a required sample size of 44 participants for each VE. At the
beginning of the experiment, 76 participants were involved; later, twelve of them were excluded
because of vision problems, virtual reality cybersickness, or not participating in the second VE
experiment (IVE or DTVE). A total of 60 university students, 37 females, and 23 males,
participated in both experiments voluntarily from ID. Bilkent University. The age range of the
participants was 19 to 30 years. Ishihara's electronic color blindness test was used (Color-
blindness.com, 2019) to check whether the participants had an intact color perception before
the experiment.
3.2. Virtual environment and stimuli
The experimental stimuli in the virtual environment have two important features:
boundaries with various space properties. Two types of boundaries are tested, curved horizontal
boundary (HB) and curved vertical boundary (VB). Four walls bound HB space, and the
boundaries of each wall are connected with horizontal concave connections. There is no 90-
degree edge in the horizontal plane of the space as there are in standard room connections. Four
walls bound VB space, and the boundaries of each wall are connected to the ceiling as vertically
concave links. There is no 90-degree connection between vertical walls and ceiling as standard
space connections. Each boundary type involves four space properties (size, light, texture, and
color) of the surrounding surfaces, where each space property is composed of two intensity
7

levels, high and low. For size, the levels were small (S) and large (L); for light, the levels were
dim (D) and bright (B); for texture, the levels were longitudinal (LT) and lateral (LR), and for
color, the levels were cool (C) and warm (W) as shown in Figure 1. This study's 32 VE
visualizations are designed with various architectural properties.

3.3. Design and Procedures
The study aims to identify the differences in participants’ aesthetic experience perception
of the two VEs and the impacts of curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties
on different VEs. The study was conducted in two VEs: (1) an immersive virtual environment-
IVE and (2) a desktop-based virtual environment-DTVE. While immersive, high-end VR
system displays the stereoscopic images of a digital model, non-immersive, low-end VR system
displays the monoscopic perspective views of a digital model (Bertol, 1997; Paes, Irizarry, &
Pujoni, 2021). Figure 2 presents the experiment setup scheme.
Figure 2. Experiments setup scheme
The study involves 32 VE visualizations with various space variables to be tested by 60
participants. The experiment for each participant had two steps. Each participant started the
experiment in one of the steps and then moved to the other. The 30 participants initially
experienced the IVE and then the DTVE, while the other 30 participants initially experienced
the DTVE and then the IVE to eliminate the order effect.
Participants rated these visualizations based on the related findings of the previous research
(Elver Boz et al. 2022), which categorized the three dimensions of the aesthetic experience of
interior spaces as familiarity, excitement, and fascination. After evaluating the last environment
in each step, participants completed the presence questionnaire (PQ) that is adapted from the
studies of Paes (2019) and Paes, Irizarry, and Pujoni (2021).
10

3.4. Instruments
The three aesthetic experience dimensions of thirty-two 360-degree perceived spaces are
determined using IVE (HTC Vive Pro) and DTVE (IntelI Core i7-7700U CPU @ 3.60GHz
3.60 GHz). IVE, as a fully immersive environment, provides a headset and two touch controllers
for perceiving the environment and evaluating familiarity, excitement, and fascination
dimensions as also PQ scores. DTVE, as a monitor-based VR system, was a high-performance
32" full HD monitor for the presentation of the VR environments and a computer mouse as an
interaction between the virtual environment and the user. Also, the same desktop computer is
used by all participants (Luminance 120; Gamma 2.2; Color temperature 6500K; Color display
24-bit) to prevent differences in perception due to different computer settings (EIZO, 2021;
Federal Agencies Digital Guidelines Initiative, 2016) in the IVE participant putting on the
headset and being able to turn 360 degrees as an egocentric framework. In the DTVE, the
participant was sitting in front of a desk interacting with the DTVE, using the 32” full HD
monitor and the mouse.
The IVE experience process lasted 25 to 30 minutes, depending on the perceiving duration
and assessment of presence in spaces, and the DTVE experience process lasted approximately
15 to 20 minutes on the Qualtrics. Qualtrics survey is conducted in both VEs ("Qualtrics XM -
Experience Management Software," 2021). The visualizations are randomly assigned in the
Qualtrics, and the participants rated the three dimensions of aesthetic experience on a 7-point
Likert scale after perceiving each space. Also, a week after completing the first step, the
participants were invited once more to participate in the second step of the experiment. After
completing 32 visualizations in each VE, participants were given a PQ to collect their perceived
level of presence during the 3D perception tasks in the VEs (IVE and DTVE). The presence
questions are predominantly based on the SUS (Slater-Usoh-Steed) instrument developed by
Usoh et al. (2000). Paes (2019) created a collection of VE presence questions adapted from
11

Usoh et al., 2000, Witmer & Singer, 1998, and Zikic, 2007. Slater (1999) defined the three
aspects of virtual presence: 1) the sense of being in the virtual environment, 2) the degree to
which the virtual environment becomes the dominant reality, and 3) the extent to which the
virtual environment is remembered as a ‘place.’ For that three main reasons, the decision to use
the SUS as the primary reference was informed by many studies (Paes et al., 2017; Paes et al.,
2021; Paes et al., 2023) showing successful VE presence measurements. Usoh et al. (2000) and
Slater's (1999) point of view appear to better address virtual presence as a psychological state
or ‘state of consciousness’ resulting from virtual input rather than as a direct function of system
properties (Paes et al., 2021). This study uses Presence Questionnaire adapted from Paes (2019,
pp. 129-130).
3.5. Data analysis
The study assesses the boundary type (horizontal and vertical), VEs (IVE and DTVE), and
their relationships of the three PC aesthetic experience dimensions based on the ratings of the
60 participants. The study ran a 2 (Boundary type: horizontal and vertical) x 2 (Presentation
mode: IVE and DTVE) repeated measures ANOVA for each aesthetic preference dimension.
Also, the study conducted hierarchical multiple regression analysis to determine the percentage
of the variance of the architectural variables’ dimensions in the presence score.
4. Results
4.1. Aesthetic experience dimensions and VEs
In Figure 3, the ANOVA on the familiarity dimension showed a main effect of VEs
(F(1,59)=15.81, p<0.0001, ηp2=0.21). IVE (m=3.83, sd=0.11) was more familiar than DTVE
(m=3.36, sd=0.11). The excitement dimension showed a main effect of VEs (F(1,59)=4.56,
p<0.05, ηp2=0.07). IVE (m=3.75, sd=0.09) was found to be more exciting than DTVE (m=3.56,
sd=0.09). The fascination dimension showed no main effect of VEs (F(1,59)=1.78, p=0.18)

4.3. Curvilinear boundaries and VEs interactions in aesthetic experience dimensions
In Figure 5, ANOVA on familiarity (F(1,59)=0.53, p=0.47) and fascination (F(1,59)=1.73,
p=0.19) dimensions showed no significant interaction between boundaries and VEs. The
excitement dimension showed a significant interaction between boundaries and VEs
(F(1,59)=5.93, p<0.01, ηp2=0.09). The horizontal curvilinear boundaries were found
marginally significantly more exciting than the vertical curvilinear boundaries for the IVE
(t(59)=-1.86, p=0.07), whereas the two boundary types did not significantly differ from each
other in terms of excitement for the DTVE (t(59)=0.84, p=0.40).

4.4. Presence of VEs in aesthetic experience dimensions
The presence scores differed between IVE and DTVE, with higher values found in IVE
(Figure 6). The Cronbach's Alpha mean reliability of ten items of the presence scores for the 32
IVE is 0.887, and DTVE is 0.889. Pairwise comparisons showed that the mean presence scores
differ significantly (t(9)=9.731,with two-tailed p<0.0001). The mean IVE score was 4.59
(sd=0.65), and DTVE mean score was 2.89 (sd=0.34). Item-based results and the significant
values are shown in Appendix A.
14

In Figure 7, there is a significant difference between IVE and DTVE (t=10.97, df=59
p<0.0001). A paired t-test on familiarity, excitement, and fascination dimensions showed the
paired samples between IVE (m=4.58, sd=1.06) and DTVE (m=2.77, sd=1.02). The average
difference between the paired IVE and DTVE mean values is 1.81.

4.5. Hierarchical multiple regression on VE’s and presence score
Hierarchical multiple regression was used to identify the predictive role of aesthetic
dimensions of architectural variables in determining the presence score in IVE and DTVE. Two
models were found to be effective in IVE. The first IVE model included the familiarity and
excitement dimensions of the architectural variables (Table 1). The excitement dimension
(β=0.53, t=4.37, df=57, p<0.001) is the only predictor that explains 24.34% of the variance of
the architectural variables in the presence score of model 1 in IVE. The second model of IVE
included the architectural variables’ familiarity, excitement, and fascination dimensions. The
fascination dimension (β=0.45, t= 2.69, df=56, p=0.009) is the only predictor that explains
8.35% of the variance of the architectural variables in the presence score of model 2 in IVE.
However, one model was effective in DTVE, including the familiarity and excitement
dimensions of the architectural variables. The excitement dimension (β=0.33, t=2.6, df=57,
p=0.012) is the only predictor that explains 10.18% of the architectural variables' variance in
the model's presence score, as seen in Table 1.

To summarize the hierarchical multiple regression results, the excitement dimension was
the leading predictor in IVE. The fascination dimension was the second effective predictor in
IVE. However, the excitement dimension was the only predictor in DTVE. VE’s excitement
dimension (wideawake, excited, frenzied, jittery, contended) was the common predictor of the
presence score in both environments.
5. Discussion
5.1. Effects of VEs on aesthetic experiences
Most human behavior studies aim to understand perception differences between VE and
the real world (Brade et al., 2017; De Kort et al., 2003; Kuliga et al., 2015). Also, previous
studies using simulated built environments have shown different perceptions of IVE and DTVE
(Higuera-Trujillo et al., 2017; Paes et al., 2017; Paes et al., 2021; Paes et al., 2023; Shu et al.,
2019). However, these studies have measured the differences in users’ sense of presence and
immersion between the two VEs. Besides perception and preference, the aesthetic experience
of the VEs needs to be investigated more extensively in the literature. Hepperle and Wölfel
(2023) studied a systematic scoping review of human behavioral studies that analyze VR
17

settings in three categories: perception, interaction, and sensing and reconstruction of reality.
However, they recorded only one study in their literature review on the sensing and
reconstruction of reality category related to aesthetic experience in VE facade design
(Verwulgen et al., 2019). Verwulgen et al. (2019) reported no differences in the aesthetic
experiences of subjects who were exposed to drawings and to the same models in VR.
The present study examines users’ aesthetic experience and presence results within the
related VEs. As a result of the study, the familiarity and excitement components are highly
significant factors in both VEs. The familiarity dimension of the aesthetic experience spans
elements that are a priori categorized by Elver Boz et al. (2022) as ‘pleased, happy, satisfied,
pleasant, relaxed, like to spend time, prefer to live, enjoy exploring, and others’. The familiarity
dimension may also be conceptually related to the ‘hominess’ dimension proposed by Coburn
et al. (2020), in which they investigate the human aesthetic experience by manipulating
different architectural variables. The familiarity dimension may represent belonging to a space
like home. Specifically, in the IVE, familiarity aesthetic components are higher results than in
DTVE in this study. The reason may be that IVE makes the participant feel closer and ‘like
home’ than the DTVE. It may be because the participants can experience the places without
any external factors or interruption. Also, another reason may be that while in the IVE,
participants were allowed to move around themselves, while in the DTVE.
In contrast, participants were seated and not allowed to walk during the experiment. For
that reason, DTVE is a less familiar way to explore and visualize a room than moving around.
Participants may feel in a familiar space because of the focus vision in the IVE. In addition,
excitement aesthetic components show the same result as the familiarity components. Elver
Boz et al. (2022) emphasized excitement as ‘contended (satisfied).’This finding is consistent
with Imamoğlu (2000), suggesting that more familiar stimuli may appear relatively more
predictable, satisfying, and less complex. However, fascination with aesthetic components is
18

expressed as ‘complex’ by Elver Boz et al. (2022). The fascination with aesthetic experience
differs from the other two aesthetic scales, and no significant factors exist. Imamoğlu (2000)’s
study supports this study's findings.
5.2. Effects of curvilinear boundaries on aesthetic experiences
Elver Boz et al. (2022) controlled curvilinear boundary types and space properties in their
research one by one. As a result of their findings, horizontal boundaries were found to be more
familiar and exciting than vertical boundaries. The interior spaces that are larger, brighter, and
cooler in color were found to be more familiar than those smaller in size, dimmer in light, and
warmer color. Also, the interior space with larger size, brighter light, and but warmer in color
was more exciting than spaces with smaller size, dimmer light, and cooler colors. However, one
of the aesthetic components, the fascination dimension, was affected by none of the
architectural variables controlled in their studies. Also, Elver Boz et al. (2022) proposed that
combining the boundary types and space properties, which means a holistic approach, allows
'fascination' with aesthetic components that interact with the perception of the built
environment.
Chuquichambi et al. (2022) stated that while human curvature preference is common, it is
not universally constant or invariant. Furthermore, Djebbara and Kalantari (2023) demonstrated
a negative relationship between curvature preference and possible interactions with an object.
Consequently, instead of studying architectural variables in isolation, our study examines
architectural variables in a combination way. This result is also consistent with the real-life
examples that various architectural properties such as curvilinear boundaries, size, light,
texture, and color have existed in our living environment. This study investigates the impacts
of curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties combined. As a result of the
study, all three aesthetic components are highly significant factors.
19

Familiarity and complexity are consistently perceived as independent dimensions of the
physical environment (Alexander, 2002; Kaplan & Kaplan, 1989; Salingaros, 2007). As a result
of this study, horizontal boundaries with various space properties were more familiar than
vertical boundaries and vertical boundaries were found more exciting and fascinating than
horizontal boundaries. This finding suggests that familiar things and unexpected different ones
are perceptually salient qualities of the built environment that can be manipulated independently
in architectural design strategies (Coburn et al., 2020).
5.3. Interactions of curvilinear boundaries with aesthetic experiences
Elver Boz et al. (2022) emphasized interactions between boundary types and space
properties such as size, light, texture, and color one by one. Elver Boz et al. (2022) found the
interaction of boundary and size and the interaction of boundary and light in the excitement
dimension; the interaction of boundary and texture in the familiarity dimension, and no
interaction between boundary and color.
Furthermore, this study explores the curvilinear boundaries with various architectural
properties and VEs interactions in each aesthetic experience dimension. Only the excitement
dimension showed the main effect of interactions between VE and boundary. This finding is a
main contribution to the present literature since no research analyzing aesthetic experiences in
VEs with combined architectural variables has yet to be found.
5.4. Effects of presence in VEs on aesthetic experiences
Mainly in this study, whether VE’s presence differences and similarities are investigated
with aesthetic experience dimensions. As a result of the study, the data showed that IVE is
more presence feeling than DTVE. In the related literature, Elver Boz et al. (2022) only focus
on IVE in their studies, and research needs to be conducted in the literature concentrating on
space with curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties in VEs presence
comparison. This study expands the VE’s presence feelings with the human psychology of
20

aesthetic assessments. This research provides a deeper analysis of what happens when a user
reports of VEs about presence. Identifying mechanisms of aesthetic judgments is a better
understanding of virtual models through immersive visualization.
6. Conclusion
This study makes significant contributions by analyzing the current state of VEs
literature. The study findings mainly contribute to three areas: (1) the relationship between the
VEs and the three main aesthetic experience dimensions. (2) the relationship between the
curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties and the three main aesthetic
experience dimensions. (3) the interaction between VEs and curvilinear boundaries with
various architectural properties and the dimensions of the three main aesthetic experiences.
The acquired knowledge of this research has many implications for the built environment.
The familiarity and excitement experiences increase in IVE. Also, the familiarity experience
increases in horizontal curved boundaries and excitement and fascination dimensions increase
in vertical curved edges. In line with this result, designers can manipulate this idea in the
existing spaces that include different architectural variables. These results can be substantial for
renovating the built environment.
The study provided immersive and non-immersive virtual environments relations regarding
curvilinear boundaries with various architectural properties. As a result, virtual worlds
presented in an IVE are more comparable to real-world situations than to computer screens
(DTVE). This finding supports the study that an immersive environment is more suitable than
a non-immersive one for conducting experiments in human behavioral studies. This finding
may be useful information for designers and researchers looking to create more immersive and
realistic virtual experiences.
21

Nevertheless, there were limitations in this study as the range of age analysis was restricted
up to 30, thereby not offering a comprehensive understanding of the aesthetic experience of
interior spaces in older age groups. Also, not considering the inequality of educational
opportunities since all participants were university students, the aesthetic experience of interior
spaces might have been challenging for certain age groups. The limitations could mean that the
effect of education on the aesthetic experience of interior spaces may have been partially
reflected in the study. These limitations imply that future research should consider a broader
age range and reflect the inequality of educational opportunities.
As potential directions for future research, VR studies focusing on the aesthetic experience
of interior spaces across a broader age spectrum are essential, along with inquiries exploring
the relationship between education levels and aesthetic experience. Furthermore, based on the
findings of this study, proposals for research into the application of virtual environments and
space properties of interior spaces to understand aesthetic experiences are encouraged.
Moreover, future works may include new space properties to differentiate the various
visualizations of interior spaces. For instance, in this study, the surrounding surfaces' space
properties (size, light, texture, and color) are composed of two intensity levels. However,
different space properties with many levels of intensity may be explored in further investigation.
